reading.identification: A single bay of the row of tiny lean-to booth houses (the historic tripe-sellers' 'penshuisjes') built against the Groentenmarkt flank of Ghent's late-Gothic Groot Vleeshuis, c. 1407-19: a 4.3 m wide, 2.6 m deep limestone shop house, currently enclosed within the hall's restoration hoarding.
reading.notes:
Material: the wall inside the outline is clearly weathered coursed limestone (Tournai/Balegem), not brick — visible at full resolution in set B image 0 above the hoarding. The enum has no stone class; 'concrete' is the correct ITU-R P.2040 stand-in for stone masonry at 28 GHz (eps_r ~5-7), whereas 'marble' should be reserved for polished cladding. Trim is the same lithology as the wall (stone dressings, sills, jambs), so it takes the same class. roughness_mm 9 carries the 1-10 cm regime — eroded rubble coursing and deeply recessed/washed-out mortar joints — as a scattering parameter, NOT as mesh; do not tessellate the joints.

Evidence discipline: only material is marked seen. The stone-mullioned lights, moulded sills and horizontal drip courses legible in set B belong to the parent hall's flank and roof dormers above this polygon, not to the booth itself, whose entire frontage is behind the white picket hoarding. Set A (Google 3D tiles) is a melted mush here and resolves nothing — it corroborates only that the square is enclosed and that spiky gabled forms sit on the far side.

Height: height_source is 'no-data', so 9.0 m is a fallback, not a measurement. I have not overridden it. Storey heights (3.0 + 2.6 = 5.6 m of wall) leave ~3.4 m of steeply-raking shed roof abutting the hall's flank, which is what the low slate lean-tos at the base of the wall in image 0 actually look like. Do not render 9 m of vertical wall on a 2.6 m deep footprint — it would read as a visible primitive from any rotated camera.

Roof marked inferred deliberately: set B is the weak evidence for roof form per the brief, and although low lean-to slate planes are visible at the wall base I cannot certify which annexe polygon they belong to. Shed with the high edge against the hall (south/inboard) and the eaves to the square; ridge line parallel to the frontage.

Cornice false is a consequence of the abutment — a lean-to against a taller hall gets a stone coping and eaves course, not a returned cornice. Sills and string courses are true on the prior for this fabric and are corroborated by the surrounding hall stonework. Balconies false with high confidence: nothing in this typology or on this square carries one.

Detail budget: spend it on the ground floor and the openings — the timber stall front, the deep stone reveals (~0.4-0.5 m walls), the sill and lintel wedges, and the eaves/coping edge. These are the >10 cm features that set street-level field on a 0.1 m setback. The upper wall and the roof plane deserve very little.

Scene context, important: fronting_street is pedestrian with car_access 'none' and paving_stones. Do NOT place parked or moving vehicles on Groentenmarkt. Populate instead with market stalls, cafe terrace tables and chairs, bins, bollards and dense bike parking, which is what this square actually carries. The yellow scaffolding, the tower crane and the white picket hoarding in both photographs are a temporary works state and must not be modelled as permanent fabric.

reading.identification: Early-19th-century plastered neoclassical (Empire) corner mansion at Groentenmarkt/Pensmarkt in Ghent, three storeys under a slate gabled roof, upper elevation ordered by giant pilasters and a dentilled cornice, now a Europabank branch whose ground floor has been reglazed as continuous bank frontage between rusticated piers.
reading.notes:
BAY COUNT CAVEAT — this is the field most likely to be misapplied. count=3 is scoped to the 10.4 m fronting Pensmarkt frontage, where set B/0 shows exactly three window columns inside the magenta outline. The photographed long elevation is the Groentenmarkt return along the 32.7 m footprint side and carries roughly 9-10 bays. Both readings give the same ~3.4 m bay pitch; if the generator applies bays to a facade other than the 10.4 m one, rescale by pitch, do not reuse the integer.

MATERIAL MAPPING — OSM says building:material=plaster and the photos confirm smooth painted lime render, but the enum has no plaster entry. wall=concrete is the closest dielectric stand-in for rendered masonry (ITU concrete eps'~5.24 sits near lime render over brick); it is a substitution, not a claim that the wall is concrete. trim=marble represents the polished grey-green stone plinth and pier bases at the ground floor, which set B/0 resolves clearly and which is the surface the street-level beam actually hits. Roughness 0.8 mm: upper walls are flat painted render (~0.5), lifted slightly because the ground-floor piers carry incised ashlar joint lines of 5-10 mm depth. Those grooves are deliberately NOT geometry — they are 1 cm regime and would produce specular garbage if meshed.

GEOMETRY WORTH BUILDING (>10 cm, in priority order): the entablature/string course over the shopfront (~40-50 cm projection, strongest single horizontal scatterer at pedestrian head height); the main dentilled cornice at eaves (~50-60 cm); giant-order pilasters spanning the two upper floors (~10-15 cm projection, ~0.6-0.8 m wide, they set the vertical rhythm and are visible from every rotation angle); window reveals and the bracketed moulded sills at the piano nobile; the pedimented end bay on the Groentenmarkt elevation (visible top right in set B/1). Skip the dentil teeth as individual solids - they are ~5-8 cm, wrong regime; fold them into the cornice profile.

STOREY PROPORTION — the two upper floors are unequal: piano nobile ~4.2 m with ~3.0 m windows, top floor ~3.4 m with ~2.2 m windows. upper_height_m=3.8 is their mean. Likewise window height 2.8 m is weighted to the dominant piano nobile; the top row is nearer 2.2 m. If the generator supports per-storey override, use the split.

ROOF — marked inferred, not seen. Set A's mesh shows a large dark slate plane behind the cornice but dissolves its edges; set B cannot see over the cornice at all. Form and material are from the OSM record; ridge_parallel_to_street follows the footprint (ridge along the 32.7 m Groentenmarkt axis). Height 16.9 m is flagged height_source=conflict-photo: my storey stack puts eaves at ~11.9 m, leaving ~5.0 m of roof over the 14.3 m depth, i.e. ~35 degrees, which is consistent for slate. Treat the eaves line as the more reliable number.

CLUTTER — fronting_street is pedestrian with car_access=none, so place NO vehicles here. Both photos show what actually occupies this pavement: leaning bicycles and a bike stand against the plinth, wheelie bins at the corner, A-boards and poster panels inside the glazing. Set B/0 shows a mature street tree roughly 1.5-2 m off the facade whose canopy screens the upper bays; at 28 GHz in leaf that is a significant seasonal attenuator directly in the near field of this facade and should be instanced, not omitted as scenery.

reading.identification: Groot Vleeshuis, Ghent: a late-Gothic (1407-1419) brick and Tournai-bluestone civic butchers' hall, one great storey under a very tall steep slate roof, its Vleeshuistragel flank articulated by the 16 small stepped-gable penshuisjes of the 1540s, now in public market / regional-produce-centre use.
reading.notes:
SET B IS A DIFFERENT BUILDING - discarded. It shows a ~12 m wide, two-storey yellow machine-brick block with a slate mansard, pedimented dormer, segmental brick relieving arches and a "'t STAPELhuis" fascia sign. That is incompatible with a 58.5 m frontage, 72.1 x 12.9 m footprint, 16.0 m confirmed height, building=public hall. The street photo is mis-georeferenced; none of its wall material, window size, sill or ground-floor evidence has been used. Consequently every field except roof form is inferred from knowledge of the Groot Vleeshuis, and confidence is capped accordingly.

SEEN (set A only, massing scale): one long unbroken steeply-pitched slate roof plane whose ridge runs the length of the block, i.e. parallel to both Vleeshuistragel and the Groentenmarkt frontage; a repeating fine-grained file of small gabled units with dark window openings along the flank, roughly 3.5-4 m on centre; a continuous low plinth at ground level. The plate cannot resolve mullions, reveal depth, bond or stone dressing, and it crops the right-hand end of the range, so the bay count is a reconstruction, not a tally.

GRAMMAR NOTES:
- storeys=1 honours building:levels=1 and is physically right: one great hall volume, not stacked floors. 7.0 m eaves plus the roof accounts for the 16.0 m confirmed height. upper_height_m is unused at count=1 and is a placeholder in range.
- The 16 bays are the penshuisjes, each a narrow attached unit with its own stepped gablet standing proud of the hall's flank wall. These gablets are the most important geometry on this building - they are the silhouette and what a rotated camera sees, and they sit firmly in the >10 cm explicit-geometry regime. Do not flatten them into texture on a long box; that is the visible-primitive failure this facade is most exposed to. roof.form=gabled describes the main hall roof only; the gablet range must come from the bay rhythm.
- reveal_class=deep is structural, not a photo guess: medieval load-bearing brick with bluestone surrounds gives ~0.25 m returns. Those reveals plus sills and the string course at gablet springing are the wedges that will dominate off-specular scatter into Vleeshuistragel at 3.8 m standoff.
- trim=marble is the enum's closest dielectric stand-in for Tournai bluestone (dense carboniferous limestone) used for plinth, window surrounds, sills, string courses and gable copings. Not decorative marble.
- roughness_mm=6 covers hand-made brick with weathered recessed joints and the coursing of the stone dressings. This is the 1-10 cm regime and must stay a roughness/scattering coefficient - do not mesh the bond.
- ground_floor=institutional_portal reflects the monumental arched hall entrance on the Groentenmarkt front. The Vleeshuistragel flank at ground level is largely closed backs and small doors of the penshuisjes, so detail placed against the fronting path should read closer to blank-with-small-doors, reserving the portal for the market frontage.
- Clutter: fronting_street is a 3.8 m gravel path with car_access=none, inside Ghent's pedestrianised medieval core. Place no vehicles. Appropriate clutter is pedestrian - bicycles leaned and racked, bollards, waste bins, cafe seating and A-boards spilling from the Groentenmarkt side, wear on the gravel. The black VW in set B belongs to a different city block.

reading.identification: Late-medieval Ghent grain storehouse (the Graanspijker adjoining the Groot Vleeshuis on the Pensmarkt), three tall storage levels in rubble stone with brick repair, steep tiled gable end fronting the Vleeshuistragel service alley, now a heritage-listed utility structure under scaffold rather than a dwelling or shop.
reading.notes: Wall class follows OSM building:material=brick and is not contradicted, but set B plainly shows grey coursed rubble limestone over a brick-patched lower zone; roughness_mm=9 encodes that eroded-joint rubble rather than a tidy brick face, and trim=marble is standing in for Balegem/Doornik natural stone dressings and gable coping (no limestone slot in the enum). Ground floor is screened in both photographs by white hoarding, a yellow scaffold run and heavy ivy, so it is inferred, not read: blank masonry with a small service opening, which suits a granary flank on a 1.1 m gravel tragel. Ledges inferred: openings are ~15 px at best and dressed sills are a prior, not an observation; absence of cornice and string course is likewise a judgement from the gable-fronted type. Ridge runs perpendicular to the alley — the triangular gable faces the viewer in both street photos and in plate A. Gable is plain-raking, NOT crow-stepped; the stepped gables visible to the right belong to the Vleeshuis wing and must not be copied onto this one. Storey heights are storage-scale (4.5 m ground, 3.8 m upper), giving ~12.1 m at eaves and ~5.9 m of gable rise to the confirmed 18.0 m apex, roughly a 47 deg pitch. Openings are sparse granary loops, not a domestic bay rhythm: keep them few, small, square and deeply reveal'd — the 0.6 m+ wall thickness makes those reveals the dominant >10 cm scattering feature on this facade. Clutter: fronting street is highway=path, gravel, car_access=none, so place NO vehicles on this frontage; the correct clutter is construction hoarding and scaffold poles against the wall, stacked plant and bins at the base, ivy on the lower masonry, and the cafe terrace out on the Groot Vleeshuis square to the west. Detail budget belongs on the gable silhouette, the opening reveals and the ground-level 3 m band facing the tragel; the 19.6 m rear flank can be much coarser. Note the frontage_width_m of 4.8 refers to the narrow Pensmarkt address frontage and is consistent with 3 small bays at ~1.6 m centres.

reading.identification: An early-15th-century "penshuisje" — one of the tiny tripe-sellers' houses attached to the flank of Ghent's Groot Vleeshuis on the Pensmarkt — a 5 m wide, gable-fronted dwelling in pale Balegem sandstone with a small commercial ground floor and a stepped gable to the street.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE STATUS: no field is marked seen. Set B's magenta box lands on a timber palisade in the foreground, not on any building — the projection failed, so B contributes nothing about this facade and I refused to launder its neighbours' detail into this record. Set A resolves only massing: narrow gable-fronted unit, pale grey-white against pink-brick neighbours to the right, mid and lower facade occluded by foreground tile geometry. Everything below is derived from the identification.

HEIGHT: height_source is "no-data", so 9.0 m is a default. I have read it as apex-of-gable, giving 3.0 + 2.7 = 5.7 m to eaves and ~3.3 m of stepped gable above. If the generator instead treats 9.0 as eaves height, drop to the same 2 storeys and let the gable run to ~12 m rather than adding a third storey — a 25 m2 penshuisje is not a three-storey building.

MATERIAL: "marble" is the ITU-R P.2040 stone proxy, chosen for pale calcareous Balegem sandstone ashlar (eps ~6-7); it is not marble. Roughness 8 mm carries weathered ashlar with eroded joints in the 1-10 cm regime — do not mesh the coursing. Trim is the same stone (sills, drip courses, gable coping); window joinery is painted timber but I kept trim as stone because the trim material drives the ledge geometry, which here is masonry. FALLBACK: if the pale tone in A is limewash over brick rather than stone, switch wall to brick, roughness to 4.5 mm, trim to concrete — this is my main uncertainty and the reason confidence is 0.45.

GEOMETRY WORTH SPENDING ON (>10 cm, real facets at 28 GHz): the stepped gable itself — each step with its stone coping is a horizontal wedge and the dominant scatterer on the silhouette; deep window reveals at ~0.25 m in a 0.4-0.5 m masonry wall; projecting sills; one or two string courses across the gable front. These matter far more than anything on the wall plane.

DO NOT: put brick relief, joints or ornament into geometry. Do not give this building a flat top or a crowning cornice — a stepped gable has coping, not a kroonlijst.

CLUTTER: fronting street is a 0.9 m gravel tragel with car_access=none. Place NO vehicles on the Vleeshuistragel side. Appropriate clutter is pedestrian-scale on the Pensmarkt front: parked bikes against the wall, a bin, possibly a small cafe terrace; moss and staining at the base of the stone on the damp alley flank. The alley flank is a second frontage — it should be modelled as real wall with a few small openings, not as a blank party wall.

BEAM BUDGET: two street frontages, one of them 0.9 m from a walkable corridor, means the flank deserves near-equal detail to the front. The rear is not visible from either corridor and can be coarse.

reading.identification: A shallow lean-to annex (one of the former penshuizekens) attached to the flank of the early-15th-century Groot Vleeshuis on Pensmarkt, Ghent: a 2.5 m deep stone service range with a wide timber cart gate at ground level, currently under restoration.
reading.notes:
Wall enum has no stone entry; the facade is grey Tournai limestone (Doornikse kalksteen) in coursed blocks over a lighter ashlar plinth, so I chose marble as the closest dielectric proxy (eps ~7) rather than concrete or brick. Some darker brick infill is visible in the upper wall between the hall's dormers, but the annex's own street face reads as stone throughout. Roughness 7 mm covers weathered coursed masonry with recessed and partly eroded joints - this is the 1-10 cm regime and must stay a scattering parameter, not geometry.

Height 9.0 m is height_source=no-data, i.e. a fallback. I split it 4.5/4.5 over two storeys so the generator lands on the stated total, but the annex as photographed reads as one tall gated storey plus a wall zone rising to the hall eaves. Treat the storey split as a rhythm hint, not a measurement.

The steep blue-slate pitch with stone crow-stepped dormer gablets that dominates both street photos belongs to the Vleeshuis hall itself, a different and much larger polygon. Do not attach it to this 32 m2 sliver. This building gets the low slate mono-pitch visible directly above the timber gate, sloping down toward the street with its high edge against the hall wall.

Both photos are a restoration snapshot. The yellow raking props, the crane, and the white picket hoarding are temporary and must not be baked into the twin. The correct permanent clutter for Pensmarkt is pedestrian: car_access=none on a highway=pedestrian, so no parked or moving vehicles anywhere on this frontage. Waste bins, A-boards, bollards and market stalls against the plinth are appropriate; a terrace is not, since this face is service frontage rather than cafe frontage.

Detail budget: spend it on the gate reveal, the plinth string course, the window reveals and sills, and the eaves line of the lean-to, all of which are above 10 cm and are what the 28 GHz beam actually resolves at street level. The upper hall wall is largely occluded from the corridor and deserves less.

reading.identification: A listed mid-C18 corner house at Hooiaard/Graslei, Ghent, whose street elevation reads as a historicising rebuild in the local traditional manner: four wide bays of red brick gridded by near-flush Balegem-limestone bands and mullion strips, tall small-paned windows, and an art-gallery shopfront with leaded transom lights at street level.
reading.notes:
IDENTITY: target is the red-brick + pale-stone-lattice facade carrying the GRASLEI plate and GALERIE PONT & PLAS. In B/1 the box wraps left over the grey and olive neighbours because the camera stands 1.1 m off the wall; the target is the fabric at the right of that frame. B/0 is a near-frontal read of it and is the primary evidence.

STOREYS (inferred): photos show ground + one upper only. 14.5 m as a max height cannot accommodate four storeys plus the pitched roof visible in set A (4 x storeys ~= 14.3 m eaves, no roof left). Three storeys at 4.4 + 3.3 + 3.3 = 11.0 m eaves plus ~3.5 m of gable over the 7 m depth reaches 14.5 m. Attic is habitable-plausible; excluded from count per schema. If a survey later gives 14.5 m as EAVES rather than ridge, promote to 4 storeys and re-cut the roof.

LEDGES / PHYSICS CALL: string_courses set false deliberately. The limestone lattice is the dominant visual feature but in the B/1 oblique it sits essentially flush with the brick (a few cm), which is the 1-10 cm regime: it must be carried as material contrast and roughness, not as facets. Faceting it would inject specular garbage at 1.07 cm. Real relief worth meshing: window sills (shadow line under the first-floor openings in B/0, ~6-8 cm lip), the window reveals themselves, the shop transom band, and the eaves cornice (unseen, inferred from local typology). No balconies on this elevation.

MATERIAL: wall is red handform brick with slightly recessed joints, ~5 mm RMS; roughly 40 percent of the facade area is smooth dressed stone, so the single wall number is area-weighted down to 4.5. Trim enum has no stone entry: 'marble' is the closest dielectric stand-in for Balegem limestone (eps' ~7) and is preferred over concrete. Give the stone a separate low roughness (~1 mm) if the generator supports per-class values.

WINDOWS: large multi-pane sashes, roughly 2.6 x 2.3 m in a 3.85 m bay pitch, glazing bars clearly resolved in B/0 (3-wide grid). Ground floor is plate display glazing with a leaded green transom band above; treat the transom as a separate shallow-recessed plane.

ROOF (inferred): set A shows a ridge running with the frontage but cannot resolve gable vs hip. Attached on both sides (2 neighbours), so gabled against party walls with the ridge parallel to the street is the only sensible instance. Weak evidence; do not treat as measured.

CLUTTER: fronting street is a living_street with car_access=none on sett. No parked vehicles here - this is exactly the case where a blanket parking rule would be wrong. Populate instead with leaned bicycles against the plinth, an A-board or two outside the gallery, a wall-bracket lamp, the projecting PONT & PLAS hanging sign (seen in B/1, a genuine facet worth geometry), and the cast-iron downpipe at the bay division (seen in B/0) - a ~10 cm vertical cylinder hard against the wall and a meaningful scatterer at 28 GHz.

BUDGET: this facade sits 1.1 m from the corridor, so it earns full opening-and-reveal detail; the return elevation on the second frontage is unseen and should be generated as a plainer mirror of the same grammar rather than invented afresh.

reading.identification: A four-level 19th-century white-plastered Ghent corner town house on Hooiaard/Kortemunt, six regular bays with moulded architraves, projecting sills and a bracketed eaves cornice, now in retail/hospitality use with the Barouche cafe-brasserie occupying the entire ground floor behind a green glazed-brick plinth.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE WARNING: street photo 494007850_1.jpg is NOT this building - it shows a Basic-Fit/Hans Anders shopfront under a modern concrete soffit, with the magenta box over an unrelated glazed entrance. All readings come from 494007850_0.jpg plus plate A for massing.

STOREY HEIGHTS ARE APPORTIONED, NOT MEASURED. The count of 4 is directly seen (ground + 3 upper tiers, matching building:levels=4). The 3.9 m / 3.35 m split is derived from the confirmed 16.0 m total: 3.9 + 3 x 3.35 = 13.95 m to eaves, leaving ~2.05 m roof rise over the 5.0 m depth (~40 degree pitch). The real facade is graded - ground ~3.9, piano nobile ~3.6, second ~3.4, third ~2.9 - so if the generator supports per-storey heights, use that taper rather than a uniform upper value; it is visible in the photo and reads strongly in silhouette.

MATERIAL ENUM COMPROMISES. Wall is white limewashed lime render over brick; 'plasterboard' is the nearest enum token and matches building:material=plaster, but the permittivity should be set for render-on-brick, not for interior gypsum board - the brick backing dominates at 28 GHz. Trim (architraves, sills, cornice, shopfront entablature) is moulded render/stucco, mapped to 'concrete'. Roughness 0.8 mm is smooth painted render, weathered and patched but not textured; brick bond is invisible under the render so no bond relief belongs in the 1-10 cm regime here.

BAY COUNT METHOD. Six bays counted on the top storey; the perspective run of bay spacings (270, 220, 180, 160, 140 px) is a consistent foreshortening series, confirming six rather than five or seven. Over 12.5 m frontage that is a 2.08 m pitch, ~1.2 m windows, ~0.9 m piers.

WINDOW SUBDIVISION. Glazing bars are unambiguous - mullion and transom with small panes throughout. The first-floor left bays retain leaded diamond quarries (older glass, probably a heritage retention or pub-era insert); upper floors are rectangular small-pane sashes. If the generator supports per-storey glazing patterns, give floor 1 the diamond lattice and floors 2-3 the rectangular grid. Reveal is a class judgement from the oblique view: the sash sits back behind the plaster architrave by roughly a hand's depth, clearly not a deep Gothic brick reveal.

ROOF IS INFERRED, DELIBERATELY. roof:shape=gabled comes from data. The ridge orientation is inferred from a seen feature rather than from the roof itself: the facade terminates in a continuous horizontal dentilled eaves cornice across the full 12.5 m with no street-facing gable, which for this type means the ridge runs parallel to the street over the 5.0 m depth. The roof plane is not resolvable from the pavement and plate A's tiles are too degraded to read it.

CORNER CONDITION. street_frontages=2 with a 5.0 m return. The return elevation should carry the same grammar at ~2 bays, same cornice and plinth continuing round the corner - a blank flank here would be wrong and would be visible from the Kortemunt approach.

RAY-TRACING PRIORITIES (>10 cm regime): the bracketed/modillion eaves cornice is the single strongest scattering feature on this building and must be explicit geometry, not a texture band - it is the deepest projection on the facade and it runs the full frontage. Next: the six-bay reveal grid, the projecting window sills, and the moulded entablature band above the shopfront. The green glazed-brick plinth to ~1.4 m is markedly smoother and more specular than the render above and deserves its own material band.

STREET CLUTTER. fronting_street is pedestrian with car_access=none, so NO parked vehicles - this is exactly the case where a generic parked-car rule would be wrong. What is actually seen: cafe terrace with metal tables and chairs, several furled black parasols on poles, a red A-board, planters, and bicycles toward the corner. Terrace furniture sits on sett paving directly against the facade.

reading.identification: A mid-to-late 19th-century neoclassical/eclectic rendered commercial corner block on Korenmarkt/Kortemunt in Ghent, three storeys with a giant pilaster order and dentilled cornice over a fully glazed retail ground floor, in good maintained condition.
reading.notes:
DOMINANT RELIEF, must be explicit geometry (>10 cm regime): the giant pilaster order is the defining feature of this facade and carries most of its off-specular return. Pilaster strips run unbroken from the first-floor string course to the cornice, project roughly 0.10-0.15 m, and divide the wall into three recessed panels; the ground floor repeats them as wider channelled/rusticated piers between the shop bays. Model these as extruded pilasters, not as albedo. Also explicit: the moulded window architraves, the projecting sills, the string course at first-floor level, and the crowning cornice with its dentil course (dentils as a repeated block row on the silhouette edge - this is the top edge every rotated camera will see).

SUB-GEOMETRY (1-10 cm, roughness only, do NOT mesh): the horizontal rustication grooves in the ground-floor piers, the shallow sunk panels beneath the second-floor windows, and the render texture itself. These are folded into roughness_mm = 1.0, which is a facade-wide RMS: the painted render is genuinely smooth (~0.5) and the grooved zones pull the average up.

MATERIAL CALL: no brick is visible anywhere on this building - it is continuous painted lime/cement render over brick masonry. At 28 GHz the first reflection is dominated by the render skin (penetration depth a few cm), so the concrete permittivity is the correct proxy and brick would be wrong. Colour is a warm off-white/cream. The stall riser below the shop glazing is a dark grey-blue painted stone plinth, roughly 0.9 m tall, and reads as a distinct band at eye level; worth carrying as a separate material stripe if the generator supports it.

WINDOWS: two different upper-floor window heights, which one field cannot carry. First floor (piano nobile) is the tall one at roughly 2.6 m; the second floor is noticeably shorter at roughly 1.9 m. The emitted 2.4 m is weighted toward the visually and radiometrically dominant piano nobile. If the generator accepts per-storey overrides, split them - the vertical taper is a real and legible feature of this facade. Glazing bars are true and seen: each window has a horizontal transom near the head with a small upper light, and a vertical division below. Frames are dark-painted, slim.

ROOF - weakest field, flagged. Set A is the only roof evidence and it is blurry photogrammetric mush. What is genuinely visible is a large dark slate plane sloping toward the street with a hip edge at its left, so "pitched and not flat" is real. Hipped vs mansard is NOT resolvable at that resolution; I chose hipped from the silhouette and from the unambiguously hipped neighbour in the same plate. Ridge parallel to street follows from the 7.8 m frontage against 8.5 m depth. The roof is invisible from the pavement - the cornice occludes it completely - so it matters for silhouette and for anything looking down, not for street-level facade scattering. No dormers seen on the target.

HEIGHT BUDGET, reconciled against the measured 17.0 m: 4.2 ground + 4.0 + 4.0 upper = 12.2 m, plus ~0.5 m of cornice = ~12.7 m to eaves, leaving ~4.3 m of roof to the ridge. Consistent without inventing a storey. Ground floor is genuinely grand-commercial tall; do not shrink it to a domestic 3 m.

CLUTTER - do not park cars here. fronting_street is Korenmarkt, highway=pedestrian, car_access=none, and the imagery confirms it: set B shows bicycles leaned against the plinth and a row of wheelie bins at the corner, pedestrians crossing the paving stones, no vehicles at all. The correct clutter for this frontage is parked bicycles at the plinth, bins, street trees (a mature tree stands immediately to the right in set B and will shadow/scatter across the right bays), and pedestrians. A parked-car rule firing here would be exactly the generic-plausible failure this project has already had.

DETAIL BUDGET: this building sits at distance_m = 0.0 from the fronting street with two frontages, so it earns a high budget - concentrate it on the ground-floor shop bays and piers where the eye and the beam both land, on the window reveals and sills, and on the cornice silhouette. The return elevation onto Kortemunt is visible in set B image 1 and should carry the same pilaster grammar rather than being left as a blank box side; a flat unarticulated flank is the visible-primitive failure waiting to happen on a corner building.

CAVEATS: set B is wide-lens and the target sits off-centre, so straight lines curve slightly near the frame edge - window dimensions are measured from bay pitch anchored to the known 7.8 m frontage rather than from raw pixel counts, to avoid inheriting that distortion. The ground floor is currently vacant or between tenants (green-tinted glazing with posters), so shopfront signage should be modelled as generic rather than reproducing what the photo happens to show.

reading.identification: A four-storey Ghent townhouse on Hooiaard in Flemish traditionalist / Scheldt-Gothic dress — red brick with Balegem sandstone speklagen banding rising to twin crow-stepped gables — most likely a late-19th/early-20th-century historicist rebuild of a 16th-century merchant house, now with a bar/restaurant occupying the ground floor and a terrace on the pedestrian sett.
reading.notes:
GEOMETRY vs ROUGHNESS, the key call on this facade: the brick/stone checkerboard banding (speklagen) reads as heavy relief to the eye but projects only 2-4 cm. That is the 1-10 cm regime - it must NOT be meshed, it is carried by roughness_mm=6.0 plus a raised diffuse scattering coefficient. What IS explicit geometry: (a) the crow-stepped gable copings, ~5-6 steps per gable, each tread 0.4-0.6 m deep and ~0.5 m rise - these dominate the silhouette from every rotated camera and are the single highest-value facets on the building; (b) window reveals at ~0.20-0.25 m; (c) the continuous stone sill/impost courses at each floor level, projecting ~0.10-0.15 m with a drip. string_courses=true refers only to those floor-level courses, not to the decorative banding.

TRIM material: enum has no sandstone/limestone. "concrete" (eps_r ~5.2) is the closest dielectric match for Balegem calcareous sandstone; "marble" at 7.07 would overshoot. Applies to the bands, window surrounds, sills and gable copings.

ROOF: OSM roof:shape=gabled is not contradicted - stepped_gable is a corbie-stepped subtype of it. Twin gables, gable ends to the street, so the ridge(s) run perpendicular into the 15.2 m depth. Roof form is seen in set B despite the brief's warning, because the gable is the street elevation here and is fully visible, not foreshortened.

WINDOWS: dark-framed, subdivided into multiple lights with vertical and horizontal bars - descendants of stone cross-windows (kruiskozijnen). Bars are genuinely resolved in set B image 1. Reveal class read from the shadow depth in the oblique view; it is a class, not a measurement.

CLUTTER - do not default-populate: fronting_street is highway=pedestrian, car_access=none, surface=sett. ZERO vehicles. This is the exact case the parked-car rule got wrong elsewhere. What the photographs actually show at the kerb, and what should be placed: 3-4 large square cafe parasols (~3 m, canopy at ~2.4 m), one folded parasol on its mast, ~15-20 light chairs and small tables, a row of rectangular planters with clipped hedging along the terrace edge, one or two A-board signs. Parasol canopies and planters are >10 cm scatterers within 3 m of the corridor and are worth their budget; chairs are thin-limbed and can be low-poly.

BUDGET: distance_m = 0.0, so this facade is on the corridor. Spend on the ground-floor shopfront plane, the reveals, and the gable steps. The 15.2 m flank is attached on both sides (attached_neighbours=4) and needs almost nothing.

ATTIC: a 4th level of habitable space sits inside the stepped gable with 1-2 small openings per gable; storeys.count=4 excludes it per schema, matching OSM building:levels=4.

flags: roof form marked `seen`, but no view here looks down on it

reading.identification: A tall four-storey mid-to-late 19th-century Ghent brick townhouse of warehouse proportions on the pedestrian Pensmarkt, standing on a weathered stone plinth, now in retail/horeca use with a café-restaurant behind full-height glazed ground-floor openings.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE SPLIT, field by field.

storeys: count 4 is seen (photo 0 resolves ground + three upper window rows) and agrees with building:levels=4. The 4.0 / 3.0 m split is apportioned, not measured: it is my division of the confirmed 16.0 m, chosen so eaves land at ~13.0 m and the ridge rise is ~3.0 m over a 4.7 m half-span (~33 deg), which suits the roof pitch in the plate. The tall ground storey is genuinely seen - the French windows are roughly 1.5x the height of the upper openings - so the proportion is observed even though the absolute metres are derived.

bays: counted from photo 0 by fitting a projective series to the ground-floor opening centres and checking it against the upper rows; six positions fit, giving a 2.27 m pitch. Uncertain by +/-1. The far end compresses into a few pixels and the near end runs off the right frame edge, so a seventh bay beyond the frame cannot be excluded. If the generator prefers a rounder pitch, 5 bays at 2.72 m is the alternative I would accept.

window: width and height are scaled off the fitted bay pitch, so they inherit the bay-count uncertainty; treat 1.3 x 2.1 m as the upper-floor type. The GROUND-FLOOR openings are a different and much taller type - roughly 1.4 x 2.9 m French windows with a fixed transom light over a two-leaf casement - and should not be generated at the upper-floor size. glazing_bars true is unambiguous: upper windows are four-light (one vertical mullion, one horizontal transom) and read clearly in the near-frame windows. reveal_class shallow: the jambs return into the brick and throw a real shadow, and the sills project past the wall face; the class is right, the ~0.12 m is the class nominal, not a measurement.

ledges: sills, string_courses and balconies are directly seen and unambiguous. CORNICE IS THE ONE INFERRED MEMBER of this group - photo 0 is cut off below the eaves and the plate resolves only a slight overhang shadow. I set it true on typology (a modest corbelled brick eaves is near-universal on this Ghent building type). If the group evidence flag has to be read as all-or-nothing, treat cornice alone as inferred.
  - sills: heavy projecting bluestone slabs on every opening, well over 10 cm proud - explicit geometry, worth the facets.
  - string_courses: a continuous projecting stone band runs the full frontage under the ground-floor windows, capping the plinth. This is the strongest horizontal line on the building and the one most likely to matter for street-level scattering.
  - balconies: ornate cast-iron juliet balconettes in front of the upper-floor windows, roughly 0.10-0.15 m proud. Geometry, not texture - they are open scrollwork and should be a shallow railing frame, not a solid slab.

material: brick is seen and matches building:material=brick. Roughness 6 mm is set for old handmade brick with eroded, recessed joints and visible patch repairs - photo 0 shows joint relief and spalling well above the smooth-render regime but entirely inside the 1-10 cm band, so it belongs in the roughness number and never in the mesh. trim = marble is a proxy choice, not a literal read: the sills, string course and plinth are Belgian bluestone, a dense carbonate limestone, and marble is the closest available dense-stone permittivity class. Window frames are painted timber (white at ground floor, dark brown/black above) and are a minor area; if the generator can carry a second trim, wood is correct for them.

roof: the plate is the only view and it does show a pitched red clay-tile plane whose lower edge sits directly on the boxed frontage and whose ridge, capped in orange ridge tiles, runs parallel to that frontage. That supports gabled and ridge-parallel, and agrees with roof:shape=gabled. It is a Google-tiles reconstruction, so the read is soft: the far slope is inferred entirely, and the eaves detail is beyond the tiles' resolution. Roof covering is red clay pantile, not slate - the neighbours in the same plate are grey, this one is distinctly red.

PLINTH - do not omit. The building sits on a raised rough stone plinth, roughly 0.6-0.9 m, weathered sandstone/limestone rubble, with a cellar door and a step up to the entrance. It is a different material and a different roughness from the brick above (rougher, ~10 mm) and it is exactly at the height the street-level beam illuminates. This is the single most valuable piece of ground-floor geometry on the building.

CLUTTER, and please calibrate it to Pensmarkt specifically. fronting_street is pedestrian with car_access=none. NO VEHICLES. This is the square where the parked-car rule went wrong. What the photos actually show at this wall:
  - photo 1 is dominated by a market/food stall with a heavy olive canvas canopy pitched right against the building, with lettering on the valance. Pensmarkt and the adjoining Groentenmarkt run stalls; a stall volume against this frontage is evidence, not decoration.
  - photo 0 shows stacked timber terrace chairs and a bench against the plinth, an A-frame or wall blackboard, and a wheelie bin at the corner. A café terrace footprint outside the glazing is correct here.
  - a continuous black awning rail or retractable-awning box runs the full width above the ground-floor openings, with wall-mounted spotlights and a CCTV camera on brackets. That rail is a long horizontal edge at about 4 m, directly in the street-level beam, and is cheap geometry with real scattering value.
  - photo 1 also shows scaffolding and yellow scaffold guardrails against the flank, and the flank itself is whitewashed painted brick with small barred windows - a different treatment from the main frontage. If the generator wraps one material around the whole solid, the flank will be wrong.
  - pedestrians, bikes and a tower crane on the skyline in photo 0; the crane is transient and I would not model it.

DETAIL BUDGET. The building is at distance 0.0 m from the study corridor, so it deserves the geometry: reveals, the bluestone sill band, the projecting sills, the juliet railings, the awning rail, the plinth. Spend nothing on brick bond, mortar joints or the ironwork's scroll pattern - all of that is 1-10 cm and becomes roughness plus a scattering coefficient. Small dark square recesses appear high on the wall near the top in photo 0; they are either attic vents or old putlog/anchor recesses and I could not resolve which, so I have not encoded them.

reading.identification: Mid-to-late 19th-century (c. 1860-1880) eclectic/neoclassical Ghent corner townhouse-with-shop (herenhuis met winkel) on the Korenmarkt/Hooiaard corner: painted stucco over brick, four storeys, arcaded piano nobile behind a continuous cast-iron balcony, ground floor now a cafe/laundromat (Wasbar) with upper-floor flats.
reading.notes:
Bay count cross-checked three ways: 4 arch heads on the piano nobile in the B_0 enlargement, 4 window columns on each rectangular upper floor, and 4 columns inside the plate-A target box. At the given 9.0 m frontage that is a 2.25 m rhythm with ~0.65 m piers, consistent with the photographed pier/opening ratio.

Storey stack reconciles with the adopted 15.8 m height: tall glazed ground floor + fascia to balcony level ~4.4 m, then three uppers at ~3.5 m, then the cornice/attic band. Piano nobile is actually the tallest floor (arched openings ~3.2 m) and the third floor the shortest (~2.2 m); 3.5 m and the 2.6 m window height are central values across the three uppers, not measurements of any one floor.

Windows: piano nobile openings are round-arched with radiating fan tracery in the heads, clearly resolved in B_0 — hence glazing_bars true. Uppers are rectangular, subdivided into two or three lights with vertical mullions. reveal_class shallow (~0.12 m) is a class, not a measurement; B_0 shows a consistent shadow band on one side of each opening plus projecting moulded architraves, which supports recessed rather than flush, but no photograph at this range resolves depth better than a class. The arched floor is genuinely deeper than the uppers.

Roof is the weakest field and is marked inferred, not seen. Set B is shot from directly under the facade and sees no roof at all; the dark slope above the cornice in plate A is at 3D-tile resolution and may belong to the taller neighbour. Mansard with ridge parallel to street is the type prior for a Ghent townhouse of this date on an 11.2 m deep plot wanting an attic floor. If a roof-form dataset exists, it overrides this.

Ledges: all four present and all above the 10 cm regime, so all should be explicit geometry. The dominant element is a continuous cast-iron balcony spanning the entire frontage at first-floor level, with separate balconettes at the upper windows. That balcony is a metre-scale projecting wedge directly over the pedestrian corridor and will dominate street-level off-specular scattering for this facade — do not let it degrade to a painted band. Dentil/modillion cornice at the top, moulded string course between piano nobile and second floor, projecting moulded sills throughout.

Material: wall set to concrete rather than brick on purpose. The facade is smooth painted cement render over brick; at 28 GHz the penetration depth is short enough that the render skin sets the reflection, so cement-render permittivity is the right proxy and the brick behind it is not the operative surface. roughness_mm 0.8 reflects well-maintained smooth painted render with mild weathering; no bond or joint relief to carry. trim set to metal is a directorial choice worth reviewing downstream: the architraves, sills, string course and cornice are all moulded render, i.e. electromagnetically identical to wall, so assigning them to trim buys nothing, whereas the ironwork is the one materially distinct element on the facade. If the generator wires trim to window surrounds rather than to railings, switch trim to concrete and give the balcony ironwork its own metal assignment.

Context/clutter, for whoever dresses the scene: fronting street Hooiaard is pedestrian with car_access none and sett surface. No parked or moving vehicles on this frontage — this is exactly the case the blanket parking rule got wrong on Ghent's pedestrian squares. Correct clutter is cafe terrace furniture (tables and chairs are visible on the pavement in B_1), waste bins, parked bicycles, and A-boards. Corner condition: street_frontages 2, so the Korenmarkt return elevation should carry the same storey lines, cornice and balcony grammar rather than being left blank. The attached neighbour to the right is a separate, taller white building with its own higher dentil cornice and a roughly 1.5 m cornice step - keep that step, it is a real silhouette event. The neighbour beyond that is terracotta-painted, so do not let a single albedo run across the block.

reading.identification: Late-19th-century eclectic/neoclassical commercial corner block in pale ashlar or painted render, currently a bank branch, with a tall rusticated ground-floor base of plate-glass bays and tall transomed windows in recessed panels above.
reading.notes: Evidence split within groups, stated explicitly. LEDGES: projecting moulded sills under each upper window and the heavy string course/band above the shopfront are both directly seen in set B image 0; the crowning cornice is above the top of both street frames and is inferred from the building type (a facade of this order does not stop without one). Balconies false and that is a genuine negative observation, not an omission. ROOF: set A is degraded Google-tile geometry inside the magenta box - a pale grey plane with a weak slope break behind it. Read as a simple double-pitched roof, ridge parallel to the 9.2 m frontage over a 5.3 m span (about 40 deg to reach 17.1 m from an eaves near 14.8 m), gable ends on the two party walls. A mansard is not credible at 5.3 m depth. Marked inferred; do not treat set A as roof evidence. STOREYS: derived from height_m, not counted. Both photos crop the building mid-elevation. Ground 4.6 m matches the visibly tall glazed base; three uppers at 3.4 m gives eaves 14.8 m and leaves 2.3 m of roof. If the ground floor is shorter than read, the alternative is ground + 4 at ~3.0 m; the total height is fixed either way, so the silhouette is safe and only the floor banding shifts. MATERIAL: smooth pale ashlar or cemented render, fine joints, 1.5 mm RMS. The ground-floor rustication grooves are 2-4 cm deep and are deliberately left in the roughness term, not meshed - at 1.07 cm they are in the band where facetting breaks the locally-smooth assumption. trim=concrete is a considered choice: the timber window joinery is real but a few cm wide and sub-geometry, whereas every element the generator will extrude as trim (sills, string course, architraves, rusticated piers, cornice) is the same stone/render as the wall. Assigning wood there would put the wrong permittivity on every ledge. WINDOWS: two vertical lights per opening with transoms, clearly resolved in set B image 0; reveal read as deep from the shadow depth on the left jambs plus the recessed panel between the pilaster strips, and this is a heavy masonry wall. Bay pitch about 2.8 m across the 8.4 m frontage. GEOMETRY BUDGET: this facade sits at 0.0 m from the corridor, so spend on the ground-floor pier/glazing rhythm and the window reveals and sills - that is the off-specular structure that decides street-level field here. CONTEXT: fronting street is pedestrian with car_access none on paving stones, so no parked vehicles on this frontage under any rule. Set B image 1 shows terrace seating to the left, standing pedestrians at the corner, a canted corner pier, wall-mounted CCTV, a projecting bank fascia, and tram catenary overhead. The catenary is near-resonant at 28 GHz but conventionally omitted; flagging it rather than silently dropping it.

reading.identification: Later-19th-century eclectic/neoclassical Ghent mid-terrace townhouse, four storeys on a narrow deep plot, painted cement render over brick with a giant pilaster order and iron balconettes, its ground floor converted to a restaurant frontage on the pedestrianised Hooiaard.
reading.notes:
STOREYS: 4 above ground, no habitable attic dormer visible. Heights are inferred, fitted to the 17.5 m datum rather than measured — the street photos are extreme upshots with barrel distortion, so vertical proportions there are unreliable. 4.0 + 3x3.4 = 14.2 m eaves, cornice+cresting to ~15.0 m, leaving ~2.5 m of roof rise over the 7.6 m depth (~33 deg). Ground floor is tall because the restaurant fascia sits high; do not shorten it.

BAYS: 3 bays across 7.2 m frontage = 2.4 m bay pitch, windows ~1.2 m wide, so ~1.2 m of pier between openings. Rhythm is strictly vertical and aligned floor to floor.

GEOMETRY THAT MUST BE MODELLED (>10 cm regime, all seen):
- Giant pilasters, full height of floors 1-2, one on each bay division and one at each party edge. Project ~0.15-0.20 m, width ~0.45 m, with consoled/bracketed capitals that project further (~0.30 m). These are the dominant off-specular scatterer on this wall and the single feature that distinguishes it from its neighbours. Do not paint them.
- Three cast-iron juliet balconies at first floor, one per bay, full window width, projection ~0.20 m, height ~1.0 m. Open railing, not a solid slab and not a floored balcony — model as a thin vertical grille standing off the wall.
- Continuous moulded sill/string band under the top-storey windows, carried on small consoles, projection ~0.15 m.
- Modillioned main cornice at the top, projection ~0.45-0.55 m — the strongest single horizontal wedge on the facade.
- Iron cresting/railing above the cornice line, seen in the upshot; low, open, ~0.8 m.
- Entablature/fascia band over the shopfront, projection ~0.25 m.

MATERIAL: wall is painted cement render over brick. Mapped to concrete rather than brick because the electromagnetically relevant surface layer is the render, not the masonry behind it; the joints are not exposed anywhere on this facade. roughness_mm 0.8 rather than the ~0.5 of fresh smooth render, because the render is visibly weathered, patched and flaking, especially on the pilaster shafts. Marked inferred: photos show the finish and its condition but cannot support an RMS number.

TRIM mapped to metal deliberately. The render mouldings (pilasters, cornice, sill band, architraves) are already covered by wall=concrete, so trim carries the black ironwork, which is the distinctive and radio-relevant trim here: three balconettes, the roof cresting, the dark metal shopfront framing and the projecting banner bracket.

GROUND FLOOR: modern inserted restaurant front, dark grey painted panelling with full-height metal-framed glazing, recessed entrance door, illuminated fascia sign and a projecting red banner sign at first-floor level. Classed cafe_glazing rather than shopfront because it is a food venue with continuous glazing to the pavement. Glazing is near-flush with the facade plane, unlike the recessed upper windows.

ROOF: set A only, and it is mushy Google 3D tile geometry. What it does show is a pitched plane sloping back from the street cornice, continuous with the neighbouring eaves line along the row, hence ridge parallel to street. Gabled rather than hipped follows from the mid-terrace condition (party walls on both sides, 4 attached neighbours). Treat orientation as the weakest field in this record; if the cadastre carries a roof form, prefer it.

CLUTTER, calibrate to this street: Hooiaard is highway=pedestrian with car_access=none on a sett surface. No parked or moving vehicles at this frontage under any circumstances. Appropriate clutter is pedestrian and commercial: A-boards, a bin, leaning bicycles, and the souvenir/retail spill visible outside the neighbouring unit in photo 1. The photos also show overhead catenary/tram-style wiring crossing the street above the facade.

DETAIL BUDGET: the building sits 0 m from its fronting street on a pedestrian corridor, so the ground floor and the first-floor balconette level deserve the highest resolution. The upper cornice matters for the silhouette. The 18.7 m deep rear of the plot is invisible from any public vantage and should stay cheap.

reading.identification: Mid-19th-century (c. 1850-1880) Ghent bourgeois commercial row house on the Korenmarkt: painted cement render over brick, four storeys under a deep bracketed eaves cornice, four narrow bays on a 7.8 m frontage, with a modern full-height glazed restaurant frontage and pavement terrace at ground level and residential/office floors above.
reading.notes:
TARGET DISAMBIGUATION: magenta boxes extracted programmatically - photo_0 x[174,424] y[184,618], photo_1 x[210,503] y[184,639], both top edges solid, so full height is in frame. Target = the "Belgian Burger Restaurant"/Quick frontage, between the Pizza Hut house (left) and the Twilight Sushi house (right). The right-hand neighbour is a TALLER 5-storey building with small attic openings; do not import its rhythm.

STOREYS: count=4 means ground + 3 upper. Count is seen (three diminishing upper window bands, verified in both photos). The two heights are apportioned, not measured: 4.4 + 3x3.3 = 14.3 m to cornice against the supplied 17.1 m, leaving ~2.8 m of roof. 5 storeys is arithmetically impossible against 17.1 m with any roof. Upper floors grade downward - 1st ~3.5 m (tallest windows), 2nd ~3.3, 3rd ~2.9 with visibly shorter windows; if the generator supports per-floor heights, use that grading rather than a flat 3.3.

BAYS: 4 counted independently at three floor bands in both photos. Bay pitch 1.95 m; measured window-to-pitch ratio ~0.6 corroborates a ~1.1-1.2 m opening, so the count is not a lens artefact.

WINDOW: 1.15 x 2.3 m is the dominant 1st/2nd floor opening. Top floor is materially shorter, ~1.15 x 1.5 m - vary by floor. Each opening is subdivided by a central vertical mullion with a transom light above (Belgian T-window), which is what glazing_bars=true encodes; these are not single sheets of glass. reveal_class is the one weak element in an otherwise seen group: jamb self-shadowing is clearly present in both photos, but a class is all the resolution supports - "shallow" (~0.12 m) is the modal value for painted-render facades where the moulded architrave projects rather than the wall being deeply reveal-cut.

GROUND FLOOR: full-height glazing in white-painted frames, projecting illuminated fascia, rigid awning box, open entrance, plus a separate panelled timber door at the right end (residential/service access to the upper floors) set in a grey stone surround. cafe_glazing over shopfront because it cues the terrace.

ROOF: inferred, and the honest weak point. From the pavement only the deep eaves soffit and sky are visible; the plate shows a smeared slate plane sloping back to a street-parallel ridge but cannot separate gabled from mansard from hipped at 25 cm/texel. Ridge orientation follows the horizontal street-side eaves cornice - a gable end at the street would read as a gable and does not. Confidence in the form class alone is ~0.5.

GEOMETRY WORTH MESHING (>10 cm): deep bracketed eaves cornice with pronounced overhang and boarded soffit - this is the strongest silhouette element and the top-priority facet; continuous sill/string band under the top floor; individual moulded sills on consoles at 1st and 2nd floors; shallow pilaster strips between bays; projecting fascia and awning box at the shopfront.

DO NOT MESH (1-10 cm): the render is smooth painted stucco, weathered and grubby. 0.8 mm RMS carries it. There is no brick relief to model - the brick is substrate, not surface.

MATERIAL: wall=concrete is a deliberate proxy for cement render over brick. At 28 GHz penetration is a few cm, so the render layer governs the reflection; ITU concrete is closer than ITU brick here. trim=wood covers the white-painted joinery, the shopfront frames and the timber eaves soffit, which are physically distinct from the masonry plane. The moulded architraves and sills are plaster/stone and behave as the wall material - treat them as such.

NO BALCONIES on the target. The left-hand Pizza Hut neighbour does have an iron first-floor rail; that is not this building. Horizontal lines crossing the target windows in the photos are catenary and cabling, not railings.

CLUTTER: fronting_street car_access=none on paving_stones. Place NO vehicles. What belongs here, all visible: pavement terrace with tables, chairs and planters, folded and open parasols, A-board menus, a Quick feather flag, and tram catenary wires crossing overhead. The catenary is thin but a real scatterer at 1.07 cm wavelength and reads across every camera angle.

BUDGET: 0.0 m from the fronting pedestrian street and 2 street frontages - this facade is directly on the study corridor and deserves full opening and ground-floor detail. The 16.5 m deep flank and the rear are unobserved; spend nothing there beyond the extruded envelope.

reading.identification: Late-18th/early-19th-century neoclassical rendered-brick bourgeois townhouse on the Korenmarkt/Kortemunt corner in Ghent, four storeys under a red-tiled hipped roof, now in mixed use with a bar-restaurant (Barouche) occupying a full-width glazed shopfront at ground level.
reading.notes:
STOREYS: 4 above ground, counted directly in both street photos (three window rows above the shopfront, top row tucked under the cornice and visibly shorter). Heights are chosen to close on the measured 17.4 m rather than set independently: 4.2 + 3x3.4 = 14.4 m to eaves, leaving ~3.0 m of hipped roof over the 6.7 m depth (~42 deg pitch). The tall ground floor is genuine, not an assumption - the shopfront head sits well above head height in both views.

BAYS: 5 on the Korenmarkt front. The building has two frontages; the wall turns at an arris roughly four-fifths across photo 0 and the openings beyond it belong to the Kortemunt return, so they are excluded. 11.8 / 5 = 2.36 m bay pitch, normal for this type and consistent with the ~1.2 m windows.

WINDOWS: sizes read off photo 1, which is the least lens-distorted. Representative 1.2 x 2.0 m; in reality the first floor is taller (~2.3 m) and the top floor shorter (~1.5 m) - if the generator supports per-storey scaling, taper upward. Glazing bars are seen, not inferred: the first-floor lights show leaded small-pane glazing and the upper sashes show clear mullion/transom subdivision. Reveal called shallow (~0.12 m) from the consistent shadow line down the left jamb of each opening in photo 0; render on masonry, so a real recess exists but not a deep stone-splayed one. Reveal is deliberately reported as a class - neither photo can resolve it finer than that.

GROUND FLOOR: cafe_glazing, unambiguous. Full-height glazed folding doors and fixed lights across the whole frontage, dark painted frames, green glazed-tile plinth and pilaster strips, projecting fascia carrying the BAROUCHE signage. That fascia is a real projecting horizontal and is what I am counting as the lower string course.

ROOF: this is the weakest field. Set A is the only roof evidence and it is soft photogrammetry. It reads as a red clay-tile hipped roof with the ridge running along the 11.8 m frontage, hipped at the Kortemunt end; the flattened top in the render is more likely tile-mesh smearing than a true mansard or truncated deck. Marked seen because an image does show it, but treat as the least reliable entry here.

MATERIAL: the wall surface I can see is smooth painted lime render; the substrate is brick, which is the inference. Roughness 0.8 mm RMS reflects the render, NOT the masonry behind it. Do not raise this to a brick-with-raked-joints value (3-8 mm) - that would over-scatter the whole square at 28 GHz. Note the immediate left neighbour is exposed red brick with white stone banding and a stepped gable and does deserve a high roughness; do not let one setting cover both. Trim = wood for the painted sashes, shopfront frames and doors. The green glazed ceramic plinth at pavement level is a distinct, near-specular, high-permittivity surface about 1 m tall right where the beam grazes - if a per-element material override exists, give it glass-like smoothness rather than folding it into the wood trim.

WHAT IS 1-10 CM AND MUST STAY A ROUGHNESS, NOT GEOMETRY: render texture, the tile joints of the plinth, the moulding profiles within the cornice, signage relief. Model none of these as facets.

WHAT IS ABOVE 10 CM AND SHOULD BE EXPLICIT GEOMETRY: the projecting eaves cornice with its bed mould (the strongest single scattering wedge on this facade, at ~14.4 m), the shopfront fascia band, individual window sills, the window reveals, the plinth pilaster strips, and the corner arris where the two frontages meet.

CLUTTER / CONTEXT: fronting street is a paving-stone pedestrian square with car_access none, and both photos confirm zero vehicles. Place NO parked cars here. What is actually seen and should be populated: a row of closed black parasols on masts along the frontage, cafe tables and chairs on the paving, an A-board, timber planter boxes and a wheelie bin at the left return, and bicycles parked across the square. These are the correct ground-plane scatterers for this location.

DETAIL BUDGET: this building fronts the square at 0.0 m, so it earns full resolution on the ground floor and the cornice line. Spend on the shopfront glazing plane, the plinth, the terrace furniture and the cornice; spend far less on the rear and roof, which no street-level ray reaches.

reading.identification: A three-bay, three-storey 17th-century Ghent quayside merchant's house on the Korenlei (heritage 4), brick with sandstone speklagen and stone-framed cross-windows rising from a water-level cellar, crowned by a steep slate mansard with a monumental scrolled baroque dormer; now in guest-house use ("Rooms with a View").
reading.notes:
SEPARATE GROUND PLANES: the Korenlei has a lower stone quay at the water and the street above. The three round-arched, oxblood-painted cellar doors in B_1 sit on the LOWER quay, below Korenlei level, and are excluded from the storey count (basement). They must still be generated — they are the whole base of the elevation seen from Graslei and from the water, i.e. exactly the angles a rotating judge camera will take. The ground_floor field describes the Korenlei-level storey, which is tall windows plus a house door, not a shopfront; the cafe terrace and parasols in both photos belong to the NEIGHBOUR to the left, not this plot.

DO NOT COPY THE NEIGHBOUR. The house immediately left in B_0 has a stepped gable (trapgevel). This building does not. Its crown is a mansard with one wide central dormer carrying volute scrolls, an oculus and a segmental pediment. Defaulting this plot to a Ghent stepped gable would be the generic-plausible failure.

STOREY HEIGHTS are derived, not measured directly: count is seen in both photos; heights come from scaling B_1 proportions against the supplied 16.7 m, which yields ~10 m of wall, ~5.5 m of roof, and the balance absorbed by the plinth/quay offset. Do not treat 3.6/3.2 m as surveyed.

WINDOW REVEAL is the one inferred field inside the window group; everything else there (width, height, glazing bars) is read off B_1. Reveal cannot be resolved by either image set — "deep" is the prior for a thick 17th-century brick wall with recessed stone-framed cross-windows, supported only by the shadow banding on the jambs in B_1.

DETAIL BUDGET: fronting street is 0.0 m away and pedestrian, so this facade is at maximum illumination. Spend on the >10 cm regime — projecting stone sills, the sandstone string courses banding the brick, the eaves cornice, wrought-iron balconets on the centre bay of the upper two storeys and on the dormer, window reveals and the scrolled dormer crown. The flower boxes on the sills are ~25 cm deep and are genuine geometry, not decoration; they recur on nearly every sill and are a real scatterer. Spend nothing on brick bond or mortar joints: at 1.07 cm wavelength that is the 1-10 cm regime and meshing it produces specular garbage. It is carried entirely by roughness_mm 6 (weathered historic brick, recessed and irregular joints) plus a scattering coefficient.

CLUTTER: car_access none, surface sett, highway pedestrian. NO vehicles on this frontage under any circumstance. Appropriate clutter is terrace tables and chairs, folded and open parasols, bicycles against the quay railing, bollards, and the iron quay balustrade visible at the foot of B_0.

REAR/SIDE: two street frontages, footprint only 9.1 x 5.3 m, so the flank is short and the mass reads almost as a slab. Give the corner a real arris and carry the string courses and cornice around it — a flat-topped extruded footprint here would be immediately readable as a primitive from the Graslei bank.

flags: roof form marked `seen`, but no view here looks down on it

reading.identification: A narrow-plot Ghent quayside burgher house of late-medieval footprint just off Graslei, its facade in the traditional Flemish idiom — red brick infill within a full grid of white natural-stone lisenes and string courses — three storeys over a commercial ground floor (gallery on one frontage, tea-room with terrace on the other), largely the product of the early-20th-century historicist restoration of this quay.
reading.notes:
GEOMETRY THAT MATTERS AT 28 GHz. The defining feature is not the brick colour, it is that the whole facade is a projecting orthogonal stone cage: vertical lisenes at every bay boundary and horizontal string courses at every floor line, standing proud of recessed brick infill panels. That relief reads at roughly 8-15 cm, i.e. right at the bottom of the explicit-geometry regime, and it should be modelled as actual facets, not painted. It turns this wall into a corner-reflector array rather than a flat specular plate, and it is the single most consequential thing about this building for street-level field. If it is baked into albedo, the building is wrong. Windows nearly fill each cell, so the recessed glazing plane sits behind the stone frame — model the reveal as a real shallow step (~0.12 m); glazing bars themselves are ~3 cm and belong in roughness, not mesh.

ROOF, weaker. Form and orientation only. Set A is the sole roof view and its tiles have collapsed into smeared ribbons, so gabled-with-ridge-parallel comes from the long block-length ridge in A plus the tiled pitch and street-parallel eaves in B_1. I am not claiming dormers, and the crow-stepped/crenellated parapet visible at the right in B_1 belongs to the NEIGHBOUR, not this building — do not graft it on. A brick stack is present and worth extruding; it is a silhouette element.

TRIM SUBSTITUTION, flagged deliberately. The white members are limestone/sandstone. The enum has no such entry, so I mapped to marble as the nearest stone-like dielectric. This is a substitution I made, not something the image shows. If the material library gains a limestone entry, switch it.

ROUGHNESS. 4 mm covers regular brick with struck joints. Note the wall is a two-material composite — smooth painted stone (~0.5 mm) over maybe 40% of the area, brick over the rest. If the generator supports per-material roughness, give the trim its own low value rather than averaging; the single 4 mm figure is a compromise weighted to the brick panels.

CLUTTER, and the specific trap. Do NOT park cars here. fronting_street is Schuddeveestraatje, living_street, sett, car_access=none, and both photos confirm a pedestrian quay. This is exactly the medieval-square-full-of-cars failure. What the images DO show and what should be placed: a deep dark cafe awning projecting ~3 m over the pavement (a large flat scatterer at ~3 m height, physically significant, worth geometry), a full terrace of bistro chairs, round tables and seated people beneath it, planters, A-board menu signs, a cast-iron downpipe on the facade, bollards and no-parking roundels at the base. The building has two frontages and both are commercial and busy; treat both as active, not just the addressed one.

DETAIL BUDGET. Spend on the stone cage, the window reveals and the ground-floor glazing plus awning. The attic and roof plane deserve little — no camera on this quay sees it and the beam will not either.

reading.identification: An early-18th-century (1714) heritage-listed narrow-fronted Ghent burgher house (diephuis) on the Hooiaard quay block, 6.4 m wide by 18.1 m deep, terraced between two neighbours, with its ground floor now in use as a cafe/waffle house.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE CAVEAT: heavily occluded target. Set A outline runs to y0=0.0, so the gable is cut off by the frame - storey count and roof form cannot be read there. In set B the awning hides everything from first-floor sill downward, and the outline straddles the party wall with the pale stone neighbour; the leaded diamond-pane cross-windows visible inside the box top belong to that neighbour, not the target. The 1714 date agrees: leaded stone cross-lights are 16th-c fabric, whereas set A shows white rectangular joinery on the outlined facade. Only the ground-floor function is marked seen.

HEIGHT BUDGET: 3.6 + 3x3.0 = 12.6 m of facade, leaving ~4.3 m of gable to reach the measured 16.9 m - a properly proportioned klokgevel, not a stub. Do not extrude flat to 16.9.

ROOF: bell gable (klokgevel) is the strong 1714 Flemish prior; stepped gables had gone out by then. Deep narrow plot (18.1 m vs 6.4 m frontage) fixes ridge perpendicular to street, gable end facing Schuddeveestraatje/Hooiaard.

PHYSICS: brick relief and lime joints stay a 5 mm roughness, never mesh. Explicit geometry only for the >10 cm regime - stone sills, floor-line plat band, gable cornice and its moulded shoulders, window reveals at shallow class, and the awning/terrace canopy, which is a large flat scatterer 1 m from the study corridor and matters more than any facade ornament.

CLUTTER: fronting street has car_access=none and sett surface - place NO parked vehicles. Correct clutter is cafe terrace tables and chairs, canopy posts, A-board, bins, leaning bicycles, bollards.

DETAIL BUDGET: spend on the gable silhouette (seen against sky from any camera azimuth), the window openings, and the ground-floor cafe zone. The 18.1 m flank is a party wall between two attached neighbours and needs almost nothing.

reading.identification: A narrow-plot 16th/17th-century Flemish brick-and-sandstone burgher house on the Korenlei quay in Ghent (heritage=4, 7.1 m frontage, 17.1 m to gable top), one of six attached in a listed quayside terrace, now with a café and outdoor terrace at ground level.
reading.notes:
STREET IS PEDESTRIAN, car_access=none, surface=sett. No parked or moving vehicles anywhere on this frontage — the generic parked-car rule must not fire on Korenlei. Substitute the clutter actually visible in street photo _0: a row of black branded café parasols directly against the facade (mix of open ~3 m canopies and furled ~2.5 m vertical cylinders), rattan bistro chairs and small round tables, an A-board menu, the cast-iron quay railing, and dense pedestrian traffic. The furled parasols and railing are above 10 cm and 1-2 m off the wall, so they are explicit geometry and dominate street-level scattering more than anything on the upper facade.

Trim mapped to `concrete` as the closest available dielectric for Balegem calcareous sandstone; `marble` would overstate the permittivity. Wall brick is weathered handmade with deeply raked lime joints and irregular sandstone banding (speklagen) — that 3-8 mm relief is the roughness number, never geometry.

Spend the detail budget on: the gable silhouette steps (silhouette edge, visible from every rotated camera), the stone cross-window surrounds and their reveals, the projecting glazed oriel at first floor, the continuous string courses, and the ground floor with its terrace. The party walls are shared with 6 attached neighbours and are never seen — give them nothing.

Roof marked inferred: photo _0 foreshortens it to a sliver and the aerial plate is a collapsed photogrammetric mesh. A gable-to-street stepped gable is near-certain for this frontage width, plot depth and period, and the crowning element in the outlined box reads as tiered, but I did not resolve it. Ground floor marked inferred for the same reason: the café is unmistakable, the shopfront glazing itself is hidden behind the parasol row.

Balconies false for the target specifically — the small iron balconies and pink flower boxes in photo _0 belong to the larger house to the right, outside the magenta outline.

reading.identification: Late-18th-century (Louis XV/XVI transitional) three-bay bourgeois townhouse on the Korenlei quay in Ghent, in dressed pale limestone with a slate mansard and rocaille carving, now retail at ground floor with residential above.
reading.notes:
SEEN vs INFERRED, field by field. Seen: storey count, bay count, glazing bars (multi-pane dark-painted casements, clearly resolved in set B), shopfront, all four ledge classes, wall and trim material class, mansard with dormers. Inferred: every metric number below.

Heights are inferred by apportioning the measured 13.9 m: ~10.4 m to the eaves cornice over three storeys, ~3.5 m of mansard above. The tall ground floor (4.0 m) is driven by the shopfront plus the balustrade band above it; uppers step down slightly with height, second floor a little shorter than the piano nobile, so 3.2 m is a mean.

Window dimensions are derived, not measured: 7.3 m frontage / 3 bays = 2.43 m pitch, minus ~0.8 m piers with moulded architraves gives ~1.25 m clear width. Height 2.1 m is a mean of a taller piano nobile (~2.3 m) and a shorter second floor (~1.9 m). Reveal class deep (~0.25 m) is inferred from reveal shadow visible in the oblique photo behind projecting stone surrounds on a thick masonry wall; a photo cannot resolve this better than a class and I have not pretended otherwise.

Material: wall class marble is the ITU stone analogue (eps ~7.07) for Balegem/Doornik-type limestone ashlar, chosen over concrete because heritage=4 on the Korenlei makes genuine dressed stone more likely than render on brick. If downstream evidence shows stucco over brick, concrete is the correct substitute. Trim wood covers the black-painted shopfront joinery and the dark window frames; the plinth and the balustrade are stone and should inherit the wall material. roughness_mm 2.5 is inferred: fine ashlar joints plus carved rocaille and moulding relief, all of which sit in the 1-10 cm regime and must NOT be meshed. The cartouche over the central first-floor window, the pilaster fluting and the brick bond of neighbours are roughness and scattering coefficient, not geometry - meshing centimetre relief violates the locally-smooth assumption of GO and yields specular artefacts.

Geometry budget: spend it on the balustrade above the shopfront (full-frontage, >10 cm, at ~4 m height and 3.5 m from the corridor - this is the single most radio-relevant feature on the facade), the window reveals and sills, the eaves cornice, and the mansard dormer cheeks which break the roofline silhouette. The dormers matter because judges rotate the camera and a flat-topped extrusion here is the canonical visible-primitive failure.

Clutter: fronting_street is pedestrian, surface sett, car_access none. NO parked or moving vehicles on this frontage - the Korenlei is a pedestrianised quay and populating it with cars would repeat the thousand-vehicle error. Correct clutter is terrace furniture (the adjacent Restaurant Korenlei Twee has tables, parasol and planters visible immediately right of the target in photo _1), a clipped bay tree in a planter at the shopfront corner, bollards, a signpost cluster at the left corner, pedestrians, and the retractable awning itself which is a real >10 cm horizontal scatterer at ~3.5 m height.

Weak points in this reading: roof form is the least certain field. Set A is too blurred to separate mansard from steep hipped, and set B foreshortens it; I read mansard from the steep lower slope with dormers set into it and no visible upper ridge, which is also the regional norm for this period and street. Ridge parallel to street is inferred from the 10.2 x 8.3 m footprint with the 7.3 m side to the quay. Attic storey inside the mansard is excluded from the count per schema.
