reading.identification: A c.16th–17th-century Flemish Renaissance quay house on Korenlei, Ghent — a very narrow gable-fronted canal house in brick with sandstone dressings and a crowned ornamental gable, heavily restored around 1900, now a bar/restaurant at ground level with lettable rooms above.
reading.notes:
STOREYS: set B shows ground (café, largely masked by parasols) + 2 full upper storeys with cross-windows and flower boxes, then a gable containing two further window levels. I read the gable levels as attic, so count=3. 3.8 + 2x3.3 = 10.4 m to eaves leaves ~4.7 m of gable to reach the data height of 15.1 m, which matches the two-tier crowned gable in the photos. Do not "fix" this by adding a storey — a 4th storey would squeeze the gable to under 3 m and contradict what set B shows.

ROOF: marked inferred, not seen, on purpose. The gable SHAPE is genuinely seen (both set B frames show it clear against sky: stepped shoulders with scrolled/voluted transitions and a crowning aedicule with pinnacles). ridge_parallel_to_street=false is inferred from the gable facing the quay; set A is too degraded to confirm a ridge. stepped_gable is the closest enum member — the true profile is a stepped gable with Renaissance scroll infill, so if the generator can bias the step edges toward curved shoulders, do that. Not a bell gable (no smooth klokgevel curve).

FOOTPRINT NOTE: footprint_m [6.3, 3.7] gives a 3.7 m depth, which is far too shallow for this house type and is inconsistent with frontage_width_m 5.4. The polygon is almost certainly a fragment of a deeper party-wall house. I have not contradicted the data, but do not derive roof geometry from that aspect ratio — it would put the ridge parallel to the street, which the street gable rules out.

MATERIAL: wall is orange-red hand-formed brick, weathered, with raked joints — 6 mm RMS carries the 1-10 cm regime; do NOT mesh the brick relief. trim is Balegem-type sandy limestone (the string courses, mullions, sills, gable dressings). "marble" was the only natural-stone enum member but is wrong electrically — dense calcite sits near eps'=7.1 whereas this porous weathered limestone is nearer 5-6, so concrete is the better ITU analogue. Give the trim a lower roughness than the wall (~1.5 mm) if the generator supports per-class roughness; the dressed stone is much smoother than the brick.

GEOMETRY BUDGET (>10 cm, worth explicit facets): the continuous sandstone string courses at every floor line are the dominant horizontal relief on this facade and are the single most important thing to model — they project clearly and run the full frontage. Then the projecting window sills, the stone mullion+transom crosses standing proud of the glazing plane, the deep reveals, and the stepped/scrolled gable profile with its cornice ledges and crowning aedicule. The gable steps are silhouette edges seen from every camera angle — spend there. Flower boxes sit on the sills at every level and are ~30 cm deep; they are real occluders and belong as geometry, not texture.

NO BALCONIES. The flower boxes are not balconies and must not be promoted into them.

CLUTTER / STREET: fronting street is Korenlei, highway=pedestrian, car_access=none. ZERO vehicles. Do not park anything here — this is exactly the case the parked-car rule got wrong. What does belong, at 7.7 m from the facade: a dense café terrace (large black square parasols, rattan/bistro chairs, small round tables, patio heaters, a barrel table, an A-board menu, planters), moored boats and a quay edge with bollards and railing on the canal side, wall-mounted lanterns and a projecting sign bracket at ground floor. The terrace furniture is the near-field clutter that will actually dominate street-level scattering here, more than the facade relief does.

BUDGET: this facade is 7.7 m from the corridor and the frontage is only 5.4 m wide, so it is cheap to detail well. Give it high resolution on the gable silhouette, the openings and the ground-floor café glazing; the rear and party walls are fully occluded by attached_neighbours=2 and deserve nothing.

CONFIDENCE: 0.72. Wall material, window subdivision, sills, string courses and ground-floor use are solid from set B. Residual uncertainty is the storey/attic split, and the fact that the magenta box in set B frame 1 straddles this house and its lighter-stone neighbour, so a small amount of the neighbour's fabric may have leaked into my reading — I keyed the facade description off frame 0, where the box sits cleanly on the brick house.

reading.identification: A small open-sided timber-and-metal terrace canopy (OSM building=roof, 8 m2, 4.4 x 1.9 m) lean-to against the flank wall of the Vleeshuistragel passage beside the Groot Vleeshuis in Ghent, sheltering the Leie-side seating of the Groentenmarkt beer cafe — a shelter over clutter, not a house facade.
reading.notes:
TARGET IS NOT A FACADE. building=roof + 8 m2 + attached_neighbours=1 = open-sided lean-to canopy over a cafe terrace. Treat as a roof plate on posts, open on all free sides.

HEIGHT: do not use height_m 9.0 — height_source is "no-data", it is a default fallback. A terrace canopy here is ~2.4 m at the eaves, ~3.0 m at the high side against the party wall. I set ground_height_m 3.0 as the true overall structure height; upper_height_m 2.2 is schema-mandated filler and is unused (count=1).

SET A IS UNUSABLE FOR THIS TARGET. The magenta box in the plate is the bogus 9 m height projected onto the quayside row behind; it outlines a different, taller building. Nothing in set A was read as evidence. Google 3D tiles cannot resolve an 8 m2 canopy in any case.

WINDOW RECORD IS A NULL PLACEHOLDER. There is no glazing and no wall to glaze. width/height/reveal/glazing_bars are schema-minimum filler — emit zero window instances. bays=1 is likewise degenerate: one open bay between corner posts.

GROUND FLOOR = arcade, chosen for physics not style: the ground level is open air between posts, with partial dark windbreak screens on the alley side (seen, photo 0). I deliberately did not choose cafe_glazing — that would place a specular glass panel where a 28 GHz ray should pass through.

LEDGES: cornice=true denotes a projecting eaves fascia + gutter beam ~0.15 m deep along the low edge, i.e. a real diffracting wedge on the silhouette, NOT a moulded classical cornice. No sills, string courses or balconies exist. Marked inferred: the red fascia and galvanised swan-neck downpipe clearly visible in photo 0 belong to the ADJACENT passage wall, not to the target.

MATERIAL: dark-stained sawn timber boarding for the deck, screens and posts; metal for the frame, gutter and fixings. roughness 2.5 mm RMS carries the board shadow-gaps in the 1-10 cm regime. Marked inferred — the canopy fabric is occluded by the OMER parasol (photo 1) and by the tree (photo 0). The red English-bond brick prominent in photo 0 is the neighbouring wall and must NOT be applied to this footprint.

ROOF: shed, high edge against the attached party wall, draining outward toward the quay; ridge/high edge parallel to the 4.4 m frontage along the path. Inferred — set B is weak for roof form and this one is fully occluded. Flat is the plausible alternative if the generator prefers it; both read the same at street level.

CLUTTER IS THE REAL CONTENT HERE (seen, both photos): black bistro tables and stacking chairs under and beside the canopy, one or more large dark parasols (~2.5 m, taller than the canopy itself and the dominant scatterer), dark vertical windbreak screens, a steel quay railing, and the Leie water surface immediately beyond. Populate these. Do NOT place vehicles — car_access is none on Vleeshuistragel and the surface is gravel; this is the exact failure that filled a pedestrian square with parked cars.

DETAIL BUDGET: 3.1 m from the path, so this is close-in — spend on the fascia edge, the post line, the terrace furniture and the railing. Nothing else on this object deserves geometry.

flags: storeys fill only 33% of the envelope

reading.identification: A 1726 Graslei canal-front burgher house in Ghent (date stones "17"/"26" on the facade), late-Baroque/classicising: red brick with white natural-stone dressings, three storeys under a triangular screen pediment with oculus and S-scrolled flanking wings with urn finials, on a deep 27 m plot in a terrace of five, historically a house and now with restaurant use behind a historic front.
reading.notes:
BAY RHYTHM IS NOT UNIFORM VERTICALLY. Ground and first floor carry all 5 bays across the full 14.3 m Graslei frontage. The top storey has only 3 bays, sitting under the pediment; the outer two bays are omitted there and the facade steps down left and right via concave S-scrolled wing pieces, each terminated by a stone urn/vase finial standing proud of the silhouette. This step-down is the building's signature and must be geometry, not texture — it is the profile a rotated camera will read first.

OPENINGS. Each bay is ONE stone-framed opening subdivided by a stone mullion into two lights, with a stone transom across at roughly 60% height — a Flemish cross-window in classicising dress. Each light is leaded/small-pane, so glazing_bars is dense (roughly 4x6 panes per light), not Georgian-sparse. The emitted width_m 2.0 / height_m 2.4 describes the whole stone-framed opening at first floor, which is the dominant case. Scale the top storey to about 0.75 of that height (measurably shorter in the photo), and the ground floor to about 1.1x. The white stone frame stands proud of the brick by a few cm and the casement sits back behind it — net reveal is a shallow class, around 0.12 m. That reveal is above 10 cm and belongs in geometry; it is the main off-specular scatterer on this wall.

LEDGES. sills: continuous stone sill bands under each window row, running through as string courses between bays. string_courses: yes, including the horizontal band at top-storey sill level into which the two date cartouches are set as flush raised panels. cornice: strong entablature/cornice at the base of the pediment, plus the raking cornice of the pediment itself — both project well past 10 cm and should be modelled. balconies: false, but this is a judgement call and the reason matters. Each first-floor bay has a stone BALUSTRADE APRON beneath it, sitting on the head band of the ground-floor window. These are balconets set nearly flush, with no projecting slab to stand on, so they are not balconies. Model them as a shallow pierced parapet, roughly 0.9 m tall and 0.05-0.10 m proud. The piercing between balusters is a real aperture at 1.07 cm wavelength and is worth the facets — this is a silhouette-edge and eye-level feature, exactly where the detail budget belongs.

MATERIALS. Wall is red brick, uniformly vermillion, tightly and recently pointed — a restored heritage-4 facade, not weathered stock. Joints are visibly recessed but shallow, hence roughness_mm 3.0. Do NOT mesh the bond; at 28 GHz that is wrong physics, not merely expensive. It is a roughness number plus a scattering coefficient. Trim is Balegem-type calcareous limestone, painted off-white; "marble" is chosen as the dielectric analogue because calcite limestone sits near eps 7, closer to marble than to the concrete entry. Joinery is painted timber, sage/pale green on the windows and a stronger green on the door — colour only, no dielectric consequence, but it is the strongest colour cue for the renderer.

GROUND FLOOR. A green painted timber double door in a white stone surround, reached by a short stone stoop of about three steps, so the ground floor is raised over a cellar. Flanking it are tall leaded stone-framed windows, some with amber glass. There is NO shopfront and no cafe glazing in this building's own fabric, despite hospitality use behind it — do not give it a modern glazed frontage.

ROOF, INFERRED, TREAT AS SOFT. The pediment is a screen and tells you nothing about the roof behind it. A slate plane and a brick chimney stack are visible past the gable's right edge in street photo 1, which is why I chose gabled over flat, but the ridge direction is a prior, not an observation. The 27.2 m plot depth against a 14.3 m frontage makes a ridge running back from the quay, perpendicular to the street, the overwhelmingly likely arrangement for this typology. If the generator can source a roof plane from lidar or tiles, that data should override this field. Ridge height should sit above the 11.3 m adopted height, which reads as the main cornice, not the apex; the pediment apex is roughly 13.5-14 m.

CLUTTER AND CONTEXT. fronting_street is Schuddeveestraatje, a living_street with car_access "none" and sett surface at 1.1 m. Emit NO parked vehicles here. The correct clutter is a cafe terrace on the Graslei quay in front of the facade: large square dark-grey canvas parasols on centre poles roughly 3 m across, rattan chairs, small tables, patio heaters, a windbreak screen. This is present in both street photographs and is the dominant near-field scatterer between the beam and the wall — a fabric canopy at roughly 2.5 m is not radio-transparent clutter, it sits directly in the street-level path. Also present and worth a line each: a wall-mounted lantern bracket on the neighbour to the right, a small stone stoop with an iron handrail at the door, bicycles against the quay edge.

DETAIL BUDGET. Spend it on the pediment profile and its raking cornice, the two urn finials, the S-scroll wings, the balustrade aprons, the stone mullions and transoms, and the door surround with its stoop. Spend nothing on brick relief, nothing on the cartouche lettering, and nothing on the rear 20 m of the plot, which faces an alley no beam reaches.

reading.identification: Wide-fronted Flemish brick-and-Balegem-limestone merchant/guild house on Graslei, Ghent — Scheldt-Gothic in character, C17 core reworked in the 1913 World's Fair restoration of the quay, with three storeys of stone-mullioned two-light leaded windows over a café-restaurant ground floor.
reading.notes:
BAY COUNT (seen, both photos independently): 5 window bays separated by 4 projecting brick piers. Verified by horizontal red-minus-blue saturation profile across the middle storey in each photo — brick piers as saturation peaks, dark glazed openings as troughs, at perspective-consistent pitch, with one iron wall anchor centred over each pier. Window:pier width ratio ~2:1, so opening ~0.65 of bay pitch. 5 bays over the stated 8.6 m frontage gives a 1.72 m pitch, which is tight; the footprint OBB short side is 9.7 m. If the generator can use the wider street-facing dimension, scale window width with it (up to ~1.28 m) rather than reducing the bay count — the count is the better-evidenced quantity.

ROOF (seen): NOT a street-facing gable, which is the trap on this quay. The facade ends in a straight projecting stone eaves cornice; the steep slate plane sits behind it with a horizontal ridge running parallel to Graslei. Rising off that slope are TWO brick wall dormers with stepped (crow-stepped) tops, each with a small arched opening, plus a tall brick chimney stack near the left party line. These dormers are the dominant silhouette event on this building and are worth explicit geometry — they read from every rotated camera angle and they are what the set-A plate resolves as spikes above the roofline. The stepped gable visible at the left edge of the target is the party-wall gable; the stepped gable further right belongs to the neighbour, not to this footprint. Pitch is steep, roughly 55-60 deg (inferred).

>10 cm REGIME — ask for geometry: projecting brick piers running the full height between openings; stone-framed window openings recessed behind them; continuous stone sill/string course under each window row; the projecting eaves cornice with its corbel run; the two stepped dormers; a stone pinnacle/finial on the pilaster at the left party edge (visible in photo 0). Iron wall anchors (fleur-de-lis muurankers, one per pier per floor) sit at ~5-8 cm relief — borderline, best left out of the mesh and folded into the roughness of the frieze band rather than modelled as thin metal, since thin high-conductivity slivers are numerically nasty and contribute little.

1-10 cm REGIME — must NOT be meshed: the alternating brick/stone speklagen friezes above each window row, and the alternating stone-and-brick voussoirs over each opening. These are visually the signature of the facade but are 3-6 cm relief; meshing them at 28 GHz violates the locally-smooth assumption and produces specular garbage. They belong in the roughness figure (5 mm RMS set here covers the brick field with its recessed joints) plus an elevated diffuse scattering coefficient on the string-course bands — suggest S ~0.4-0.5 there against ~0.3 for plain brick, and render them as albedo.

TRIM MATERIAL: the dressings (mullions, transoms, sills, string courses, cornice) are Balegem limestone, not concrete. 'marble' is chosen as the closest available dielectric proxy (eps ~7.1) since limestone runs ~7.6 at microwave; 'concrete' at ~5.2 would under-predict the reflection off what is a large fraction of this facade's projecting area.

GLAZING: each opening is a two-light unit with a stone mullion and a transom in the upper third, filled with small-pane leaded glass. glazing_bars true reflects real lead cames plus stone subdivision — the subdivision is the ~2-5 cm regime and should be texture, but the mullion and transom themselves are stone members of ~10-15 cm and are legitimate geometry.

GROUND FLOOR (seen, but partly obstructed): ~80% hidden behind the café tenting in both photos. Brightening the shadows resolves leaded glazing set back behind masonry piers with deep reveals and the lit restaurant interior beyond. Classified cafe_glazing rather than arcade because glass is visible but a walk-through colonnade is not confirmable; if a cadastral or heritage source says arcade, that source should win, since the two differ materially in radio terms (a large open cavity vs a flat glazed plane).

CLUTTER — calibrate to this street, do not apply a generic rule: fronting street is highway=pedestrian, car_access=none, surface=sett. ZERO vehicles. The correct ground-plane population is the terrace, which the photos show occupying the full frontage and extending 3-4 m onto the quay: two large square grey parasols/tents on poles (De Graslei, De Witte Leeuw next door), wicker armchairs, small round tables, patio heaters, a chalkboard menu on a stand, and seated people. This is directly in the beam path at street level and is a bigger scattering contribution here than anything on the upper facade. Parasol canopies are fabric over a metal frame at ~2.2-2.5 m — they will shadow the ground floor from most street-level rays and should be present.

DETAIL BUDGET: this facade is on the Graslei quay itself, at 0.0 m from the fronting street, so it earns full resolution on openings, piers, cornice and dormers. The rear and party walls (22.3 m deep footprint, attached on both sides, 4 attached neighbours) are invisible and unilluminated — extrude plain and spend nothing there.

reading.identification: Late-Gothic Ghent quay/burgher house of the 15th-16th century, brick with pale Balegem sandstone dressings, standing on the corner of Graslei and the Vleeshuistragel alley with a crow-stepped gable to the street and a cafe ground floor under dwelling storeys.
reading.notes:
Corner house, two frontages, and they are very different — do not apply one grammar to both. PRINCIPAL FRONT (Graslei, 9.3 m, crow-stepped gable): late-Gothic "glass wall" type. Near-continuous glazed bands per storey divided by slim sandstone mullions, carried on heavy continuous sandstone string courses at every floor line. Those string courses are the key >10 cm feature: four full-width horizontal wedges, project them 0.10-0.15 m. Gable copings are stone-capped crow-steps, roughly 6-7 steps per side climbing from eaves (~12 m) to apex (17.7 m); model as real stepped geometry, they are the silhouette and judges will rotate onto them. Glazing ratio on this front is high, ~70%, which is correct for the type and should not be reduced to punched openings.

FLANK (Vleeshuistragel, 16.5 m deep, 2.4 m from the corridor): almost blind. Two stone cross-windows (kruiskozijn, mullion + transom, four lights) and a poster frame over the whole wall. This is the surface the beam actually sees, so give it accurate roughness and reveal depth and spend nothing on ornament. A painted red timber/metal eaves band runs along the top of this flank at the roof springing — a small real ledge, ~0.10 m, seen in both street photos.

Storey heights are anchored: bridge parapet to the red eaves band scales to ~11.8-12.3 m against the 17.7 m datum, giving 3.6 + 3 x 2.9. Gable rise 5.4 m over a 4.65 m half-span, ~49-52 deg, consistent with the tiled plane in set B.

Trim caveat: the dressings are pale sandstone, not marble. The enum has no non-marble stone, so marble is a deliberate proxy — it renders as light dressed stone and its permittivity (~7.07) overshoots sandstone (~5.5) modestly. If a sandstone class is added upstream, swap it.

Roughness 6 mm is old hand-made brick with weathered, partly raked joints, clearly bumpy in the zoomed photo. Keep it as a scattering parameter; meshing this bond would be wrong physics at 1.07 cm.

Bays marked inferred, not seen: both views are raking and the near facade runs into the neighbour's beyond a depth break, so the exact column count is a reconstruction from the measured 9.3 m frontage plus the visible rhythm. Storey count, material, window subdivision, ground floor and gable form are genuinely resolved in set B.

CLUTTER — do not park cars here. fronting_street is a gravel tragel with car_access none, and the Graslei quay is pedestrian. What belongs at this corner, all of it visible in set B: black cafe parasols and terrace tables hard against the ground floor, bikes leaned on the white cast-iron bridge railing, dense standing pedestrians, wet setts. Set A is Google 3D tiles and is unreliable below ~25 cm/texel — it was used only for massing and the roof plane; every material, opening and ledge call came from set B.

reading.identification: A very narrow (5.2 m frontage, 4.1 m deep) single-bay brick-and-sandstone sliver embedded in the historic Graslei quay row in Ghent, café/bar-occupied at quay level, tagged building=roof in OSM and most plausibly a roofed gap or passage between the taller merchant and guild houses rather than a free-standing house.
reading.notes:
PLATE A DISCARDED. The Google 3D tile mesh has degenerated into folded-paper artefacts; the magenta box encloses a dark recess with no recoverable rhythm, openings or roofline. Nothing in this submission derives from set A.

TWO OPPOSITE ELEVATIONS. Because the footprint is only 4.1 m deep, photo _0 and photo _1 see the front and back of the same sliver. _1 is the Graslei quay front (brick + white sandstone cross-windows, sandstone string bands, Duvel terrace). _0 is the rear, over a beech hedge from a yard.

REAR IS BLIND - DO NOT MIRROR THE FRONT. Within the magenta slice in photo _0 there is no opening whatsoever: unbroken weathered brick with a single stove/flue pipe, running from the eave down into the hedge. At 28 GHz this is a clean quasi-specular masonry plane and should be generated as one. Applying the front's window grammar to the back would be a physics error, not just a cosmetic one.

WHY EVERY BLOCK IS 'inferred' EXCEPT MATERIAL. The strong facade evidence in _1 - stone mullion and transom crosses, green leaded glazing, projecting stone sills, horizontal sandstone speklagen - is legible on the immediate neighbours in the continuous row. The target's own ground floor is occluded by a black parasol and its own roofline is cropped by the frame. Sub-facts I did see inside the outline: a tall upper window with a vertical stone mullion and green glazing (so glazing_bars=true is close to seen), and brick on both elevations (so material is seen outright). Everything dimensional is prior, not measurement.

ROOF IS THE WEAKEST FIELD. stepped_gable with ridge perpendicular to the quay is the Graslei prior - the row is defined by trapgevels (Vrije Schippers, Korenmetershuis, Metselaarshuis). But the building=roof tag and the 19 m2 footprint leave a real alternative: a simple pitched or shed roof over a covered passage. Photo _0's adjacent pantiled slope and green-painted eave hint at the simpler form. If a downstream dataset resolves this, it should override me.

STOREY ARITHMETIC. 13.2 m total. 4.0 m tall quay-level ground (warehouse/guild typology) + 2 x 3.0 m uppers = 10.0 m to the gutter, leaving ~3.2 m of gable above. Photo _1 shows roughly three levels, which is consistent, but the heights are computed rather than measured.

TRIM MATERIAL. The dressings are white Balegem sandstone. Of the available enum values 'marble' is the closer dielectric analogue (eps' ~7.1) than 'concrete' (~5.2), since limestone/sandstone sits around 6-8. Chosen for the physics, not the appearance.

ROUGHNESS. 7 mm RMS reflects hand-formed historic brick with eroded, partly recessed lime joints and irregular faces - above modern brick, below rough stone. This is the correct home for the brick bond, the mortar relief and the surface weathering. None of it should be meshed.

CLUTTER - AND THE THING NOT TO DO. car_access=none, surface=sett, highway=path. Do not park vehicles here; that is the exact failure that filled a pedestrian square with a thousand individually reasonable cars. The seen clutter at this frontage is café terrace: large black Duvel parasols, patio heaters, a glazed bar cabinet, bentwood chairs and tables, wall-mounted flower boxes with trailing pink blooms, downpipes and wall anchors on the brick. Put the detail budget on the quay front, which faces the path 17.4 m out; the rear gets a flat brick plane and a flue.

CONFIDENCE 0.42. Driven by the identification, not the parameters: building=roof plus a 19 m2 footprint plus occlusion of the target's base and top in both usable photos means I am describing a defensible instance of a Graslei sliver rather than recovering this specific one.

reading.identification: Later-18th/early-19th-century painted-stucco refront on an older narrow-plot Ghent burgher house, Jan Breydelstraat, now a ground-floor interiors/linen shop with dwelling above.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE SPLIT. Set A (aerial tiles) is degraded to unusable — narrow-street photogrammetry collapse, no roof form recoverable. Everything roof-related is inferred. Set B photo 0 is the load-bearing evidence: it resolves shopfront, render, window subdivision and sills at close range. Photo 1 locates the building in its run but I cannot certainly disambiguate the target from its left neighbour there, so storey count stays inferred.

STOREYS. Marked inferred, not seen. Photo 0's outline has a dashed top edge cutting above the first-floor heads, so at least one storey continues out of frame; 3 total is the reading consistent with height_m 9.0 (3.6 + 2.7 + 2.7 = 9.0). Note height_source is "no-data", so 9.0 m is itself a default — if a real height arrives and exceeds ~10.5 m, revisit as 4 storeys, which is equally common on this street.

BAYS / WINDOWS. Two bays is directly seen: two tall windows on the first floor over a display window + door at ground. Fits 5.7 m frontage with substantial piers. Windows read strongly vertical (~2:1), white-painted frames with visible glazing bars subdividing into a small number of large panes — consistent with the late-classical refront, not with original 17th-c. cross windows. Reveal called shallow rather than deep: jamb shadowing is genuinely visible, but a moulded architrave surround on a rendered wall brings the frame forward of the full masonry thickness, and imagery cannot resolve past the class anyway.

MATERIAL AND THE 1-10 CM REGIME. The wall is painted lime stucco over brick — no exposed brickwork on this facade. Use brick permittivity for the substrate but do NOT give it brick roughness: 1.2 mm RMS for old, hand-floated, patched render, against ~3-8 mm for raked joints. Do not mesh brick relief here; at 1.07 cm wavelength a centimetre-bumpy mesh violates the locally-smooth assumption and produces specular garbage. Ornament, mouldings and render undulation all belong in the roughness/scattering term.

WHERE THE GEOMETRY BUDGET GOES. The ground-floor order is the single most radio-relevant feature and the highest-value explicit geometry on this building: veined marble/scagliola pilasters flanking the display window and door, plus the deep moulded entablature over the shopfront. These are 25-30 cm projections at 3.3 m from the street line — wedges and a shallow corner reflector directly at pedestrian beam height. Model them as facets. Second priority: window reveals and the projecting moulded sills (both >10 cm). Third: the main eaves cornice on the silhouette. Trim set to marble for the pilasters specifically; window surrounds and sills are painted render and can share the wall material.

BALCONIES. False, and this is a seen negative — photo 0 resolves the target's first floor clearly and shows terracotta planters on plain sills. The wrought-iron balconettes visible in photo 1 are on neighbouring facades to the right; do not propagate them onto this building.

CLUTTER — READ THIS BEFORE PLACING ANYTHING. fronting_street has car_access "none" on a sett-paved living_street. NO VEHICLES. This is precisely the failure mode that filled a pedestrian square with a thousand individually-reasonable parked cars. Correct clutter for this frontage is pedestrian retail: A-boards, the ornate black wall-mounted iron lantern visible in photo 0, dark fabric shop awnings (seen on the adjacent units in photo 1, plausible here), a vertical rainwater downpipe at the party line (seen in photo 1), terracotta window boxes on the first-floor sills, and small wall-mounted CCTV/light fittings above the shopfront. Sett paving should carry real surface variation, not a flat plane.

ROOF. Inferred entirely. Ridge called perpendicular to the street despite the straight classical cornice: a 4.5-5.7 m wide by 11 m deep parcel spans naturally front-to-back, and the standard Flemish pattern is an original gable cut back and masked behind an 18th-c. straight cornice. This also yields the correct raking party-wall silhouette when the camera rotates off-axis. If better roof evidence appears, mansard with a street-parallel ridge is the main alternative and is common on this refront type in Ghent.

ATTACHMENT. 4 attached neighbours, 2 street frontages — party walls left and right should be blind. Only the street facade earns this detail budget; the rear and flanks should stay coarse.
